overview: Gunaikurnai people maintain Country, kinship and cultural knowledge across Gippsland. Stoneworking traces at the Knob and exceptionally preserved wood at Cloggs Cave connect material evidence with knowledge held by communities. Their history includes colonial displacement, the survival of family connections and continuing care for land and waters.

periods.title: Native title and continuing care for Country
periods.summary: The 2010 native title determination was celebrated at the Knob, a longstanding gathering place. Community institutions, joint management and cultural learning continue a relationship with Country that predates the legal recognition.

items.text: Gunaikurnai brings together the recorded names Gunnai and Kurnai in a form agreed by the community. Different spellings in older records often reflect how outsiders transcribed speech; they should not automatically be treated as different peoples.

The Gunaikurnai Land and Waters Aboriginal Corporation recognizes five major clans across Gippsland. Clan connections place responsibilities in particular landscapes, while families share wider relationships. A single outline on a map cannot capture all those connections.

At the Knob on Brayakaulung Country, deep grooves in sandstone beneath the bluff record repeated sharpening of stone axe heads. Stone scatters, camps and scarred trees also survive, making this a landscape of skilled work as well as a gathering place.

Research published in 2024 described small fireplaces at Cloggs Cave near Buchan containing trimmed Casuarina sticks and fatty residues. Dating places these features about 11,000 to 12,000 years ago. The preserved wood provides unusually direct evidence of how people prepared and used plant materials.

Working with Gunaikurnai Elders, the Cloggs Cave researchers compared those finds with nineteenth-century descriptions of ritual specialists using treated sticks. They interpret a long transmission of ritual knowledge. The excavated objects and residues are observations; the connection across millennia is the study's argued interpretation.

Dooyeedang, the Avon River, linked high country with the Gippsland Lakes. Gunaikurnai accounts describe travel along it and foods including eels and fish. Moving through this river landscape connected meals and material resources with visits, exchange and relationships.

The Knob hosted meetings where clans feasted, exchanged goods, shared news and held ceremonies. Such gatherings joined practical provisioning with social and cultural obligations; the place mattered for much more than a single activity.

Cultural fire is guided by knowledge of the season, the place and the purpose of a burn. Gunaikurnai accounts connect fire with land health, ceremony and communication. Renewing this practice draws on Elders' knowledge rather than treating every fire as an identical operation.

During the mission era, people continued to meet at the Knob, sometimes secretly, to maintain family ties despite enforced separation. In 2010 the same place hosted the native title determination ceremony, linking legal recognition with a much older community history.

Established in 2007, GLaWAC provides a community institution for representing Gunaikurnai people and caring for Country. Its public cultural protocols recognize that knowledge belongs to people and families and that perspectives within the community can differ.

The Cultural Hub at Forestec supports community programs and cultural learning. Stories and songlines connect knowledge with ancestors and places; teaching involves relationships and responsibilities as well as information that can be written down.

ending.text: Gunaikurnai communities continue. Colonial displacement and mission control disrupted families and access to Country, but neither ended the people or their knowledge. Native title recognition, cultural learning and care for Country are later chapters of that continuing history.
